newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain debt seen vulnerable to EMU doubt short-term.
newsitem.headline: Spain debt seen vulnerable to EMU doubt short-term.

text.p: The Spanish debt market will be vulnerable to European Monetary Union (EMU) uncertainties in the short term but should be able to overcome bearishness with time, analysts said on Monday.

A Reuter poll conducted on Monday forecast the 10-year cash spread between Spanish bonds and their German counterparts could widen toward 150 basis points in a week, with peaks at around 175. But it should recover back to 120 basis points in a month.
"Rumours of a possible delay in EMU projects are exaggerated. So in a short time we'll return to a more reasonable approach," said Jose Luis Alzola at Salomon Brothers in London.
He said the spread could jump to 175 basis points within a week but then it should fall to around 125 basis points.
At around 1200 GMT, the 10-year spread was trading at around 139 basis points in what traders viewed as a technical correction from 145 at Friday's close.
The spread had shot up amid doubts of possible delays in the European single currency's start.
"Spain is not expected to delay its entry but if they put the whole project ahead, Spain will be among the most punished," said Luca Jellinek, economist at Paribas in London.
Economic fundamentals should limit the fall in debt prices.
"We are seeing a good convergence in fundamentals," said Mark Geddes at 4Cast in London. "This morning January PPI proved inflation is falling."
Spain's January PPI fell 0.1 percent month-on-month after a 0.1 percent rise in December.
Only one analyst out of 10 polled saw a delay in the launch of a single currency set for 1999.
But even the sceptic said the 10-year spread between Bonos and Bunds should find a limit at around 140/150 basis points.
"A delay is a possibility I'm thinking about for a while. Germany doesn't want Italy or Spain in EMU's start," said Alessandro Ceccaroni, dealer at UBS in London.
He added Kohl, considered one of the strongest supporters of EMU, seemed to be losing support ahead of an October general election.
If EMU were delayed, Spain's yield curve would suffer the most, with a strong flattening likely, analysts said.
The curve flattened on Monday with the differential between the two- and the 10-year bonds down to about 108 basis points from 124 basis points last Thursday.

In the currency market, analysts predicted a peseta decline in the short run followed by a recovery. They stressed the Bank of Spain was ready to dip into ample reserves to defend the currency aggressively.
"The peseta could overshoot to 85.10 per mark but then I expect it to recover," said Jellinek.
In the meantime, any possible monetary policy easing was considered on hold, analysts added.
None forecast a Bank of Spain cut in the official six percent rate at the repo operation on Tuesday morning.
The most optimistic considered a cut possible on March 25.
Others saw any rate cut later this year and were less aggressive than in the past on predictions for further easing.
"I have always said March or April (for the next rate cut), now I am saying April/May. I was expecting 25 to 50 basis points and now it seems more likely 25," said Alzola.
-- Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
